1:
Henry finds the weight of the dirge in one place: the emphasis is not on what was done but on whose hand did it. The grief is not so much that these things happened as that God did them, and that is the wormwood and the gall. To those who know how to value his favour nothing is more dreadful than his anger, since corrections in love are easily borne, but rebukes in love wound deeply. Calvin hears the opening cry as wonder at a prodigy. A people God had taken into favour and bound to himself by a perpetual covenant now appeared forsaken, which looks impossible, since God does not change with men's perfidy and the promise never rested on merit. He is careful that this is not doubt of God's constancy but a device to soften a nation grown hard under its evils, since nobody calls on God in earnest until he is humbled.

The cloud is read four ways. Gill rules out the wrong ones first: not a covering of their persons for protection, as at the sea and in the wilderness, nor of their sins, which God blots out as a thick cloud, nor the cloud that filled the sanctuary, but the black cloud of calamity; and he offers a translator's word for it, that God beclouded her. He reports a Jewish commentator who took it the other way, that God lifted her to the clouds to throw her down harder. Calvin knows that reading and supplies its picture, the potter raising the vessel before dashing it, but judges it too refined and keeps the beclouding. Clarke sees a veiling, the women of the east wearing costly veils and this one a dark cloud. Ellicott sees a thunder-cloud breaking into a tempest, and Henry sets it against the pillar in the wilderness: the side now turned toward them is the side that was turned toward the Egyptians.

Two terms are disputed. Ellicott takes the beauty of Israel for the Temple, allowing it might be the heroes who defended it, and the footstool for the ark; he insists the divine name here is Adonai, not Jehovah. Clarke agrees on both but adds a note against him: twenty-four of the manuscripts collated by one scholar read Jehovah here. Wesley makes the footstool the Temple itself rather than the ark. Clarke also quotes his old English Bible, which calls the ark his little stepping-stool in the day of his woodness, and explains that to be wood once meant to be mad.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the verbs. Swallowing carries utter annihilation, matching the word for wrath that means overflowing; and the clause about not sparing works adverbially on what precedes. With Ellicott they read the habitations as shepherds' resting-places, open villages set against the fortresses named beside them. Ellicott adds that the word for polluting the kingdom implies it had been consecrated, made unclean by its rulers' sins and their defeat; Calvin ties that profaning back to the forgotten footstool, the kingdom having been consecrated too, so that God in a manner exposed his own name to the mouths of the ungodly.

On the horn Clarke takes a figure from cattle, whose strength lies there; Ellicott makes it strength itself, standing for warriors, rulers and fortresses alike, and improves the burning clause to say God kindled a burning, like one applying a torch. Henry has the right hand turned back, so they could neither follow a blow nor ward one off. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to read these verses as a chronicle in natural order, which is managed only by forcing the figures, making every horn the frontier fortresses; the three members are a climax, not a sequence. Wesley keeps to the fire, consuming not in this part or that but round about, as flames take a house on every side at once.
4:
Clarke stages the archer: he bends the bow, sets the arrow on the string, lays his right hand on its lower end and takes aim. Gill adds that such a bow was bent with the foot, and holds God only appears an enemy through the dispensations of providence, as one afflicted man took him to be. Calvin makes the bow a part standing for the whole, so the sense is that God was fully armed; and by the right hand he understands the enemies, God having held up a banner to them and gone before with an armed hand. Ellicott sharpens it: the right hand, the natural symbol of divine power, once stretched out to protect, is now seen shooting the arrows.

Whether the likeness is only a likeness divides them. Gill reports a translator who renders it that the Lord is become a very enemy, taking the particle for reality rather than similitude, though Gill himself keeps to appearance. Keil and Delitzsch report a suggestion that the poet hesitated to say it outright and broke off his sentence unfinished, and reject it from the accents, which do not separate the words. Calvin denies the repetition superfluous. The people were so stupefied by their evils that they never turned their eyes toward God, and the truth was so hard to get into them that it had to be dwelt on, lest they take the Chaldeans for the movers of the war rather than men endued with a power not their own.

Ellicott corrects three small things. The verb is destroyed rather than slew, and takes in not only warriors and young men but everything dear. The tabernacle named here is not the Temple but the city itself, as the people's habitation. And he notices a change of gender between her palaces and his strongholds, guessing the palaces went with the daughter of Zion and the strongholds with the land; the words for mourning and lamentation share a root and chime together.

The garden comparison is the disputed place. Gill has the sanctuary pulled down as easily as a tent and no more accounted of than a lodge set up in a vineyard at the gathering. Ellicott makes it a booth of the kind raised at the feast, removed as a man removes a shed from an orchard. Clarke passes on a rendering that turns it round, the garden of his own hedging. Keil and Delitzsch hold the word means what is hedged in, so the Temple itself, and refuse the usual point of comparison: it is not the ease with which a garden or its fence comes down, and the perplexity here has bred artificial and untenable explanations. Calvin objects that cottage extenuates too much, and takes the verb for removing: God removed his tabernacle as though it were one of the little cottages watchmen keep among the vines, hiding in small chests only until the vintage is in.

What went with the building was the worship. Ellicott notes the word for places of assembly is the same as that for solemn feasts, so the ruin carried feasts and sabbaths with it, and king and priest, the two representatives of the nation's life, were alike rejected. Wesley identifies the pair as the last king and the high priest, one miserably handled and the other killed. Clarke says the ordinances were not suspended but destroyed, and that where the silver trumpets had sounded there was nothing now but warlike instruments. Ellicott hears the enemies' triumph, perhaps their own worship, standing where the festival songs had stood, and Wesley agrees they made as great a noise as those who once sang to the glory of God. Calvin measures the whole: that God should cast away altar, sanctuary, ark and festival, the very things by which his favour was sought, was as if heaven and earth had been blended together.
8:
Calvin will not let the verb behind purposed be weakened. It would be flat to say God merely thought about destroying the wall; the word means resolved or decreed, and he sets it against the false imaginings by which men persuade themselves God is present in prosperity and absent in adversity. The wall did not fall by chance. Clarke and Wesley take the measuring line the same way: not a builder's line but a line of devastation, workmen using lines to mark what was to be cut down as well as raised. Ellicott hears in it the systematic thoroughness of the work; Gill records the older disagreement about which wall is meant, the city's or the one enclosing the Temple. Ellicott alone lingers on the mourning rampart, where the very stones of Zion's walls are imagined crying out over their own downfall.

How the gates came to be in the ground is disputed. Gill has them broken, levelled and buried under rubbish, and dismisses as a mere fable the rabbinic gloss that they sank into the earth at the enemy's approach so he should have no power over them. Ellicott agrees, adding they cannot be shut in any case, the bars being gone. Clarke turns the detail into a date: sinking is what happens to gates long thrown down and neglected, so the captivity must already have lasted a considerable time, the king and princes being by then prisoners — unless the whole is spoken prophetically of what was still to come. Calvin reads the verb as fixed fast rather than fallen, so the gates proved no hindrance at all, and derides a people who had thought their defences made the city impregnable.

With the walls went the two things that had made them a nation. Ellicott says the law was practically repealed, the conditions of its observance being gone, and prophecy had become a thing of the past, the outward desolation being only the shadow of the spiritual. Wesley puts it as practice, the law no longer read, opened or observed, and notes how few prophets there were from that time until the gospel, and how few even of those living had any revelation. Calvin reads the phrase about being among the nations as meaning there was no king at all, he and the royal seed and the princes having gone into banishment.

The elders are drawn by everyone. Gill has men who sat in the gate on thrones of judgment, their opinions treated as oracles, now sitting on the ground and dumb. Henry strips them of their robes of state and puts them in the habit of mourners, seated as the friends of one afflicted man were seated with him, not opening their mouth in the gate, overwhelmed and not knowing what to say; and he will not sentimentalise the grief, quoting the Latin line that tears shed over lost property are genuine ones, since what these men had lost was their power and their wealth. Clarke makes an epigram of it: small griefs are eloquent, great ones dumb. Keil and Delitzsch have the silence come from the depth of the sorrow, the young women renouncing their gaiety and bowing their heads to the ground.

Ellicott and Calvin both find the posture a reproach. Ellicott observes that instead of taking counsel for the emergency the elders sit as though the evil were inevitable. Calvin goes further, separating the signs from what they usually signify. Sackcloth and dust were the tokens of repentance, but here they are tokens of sorrow only: the elders had no resources, knew nothing to do, and drew the rest after them into an abject and fruitless lamentation with no regard to God in it. He adds the warning that hypocrites can put on sackcloth and make a show of repenting, and that the show is a false pretence.
11:
Gill reports a Jewish commentator who put the weeping into the mouths of the elders just described, but takes it himself for the prophet's, who had wept his eyes dry, or rather blind, over calamities from which he personally gained liberty. Keil and Delitzsch broaden it: he speaks not for himself only but in the name of all the godly. Calvin makes the grief the point. In the deepest sorrow tears dry up at last, so a weeping that never ends is a sorrow which never ripens and must be very bitter; the man who once asked who would turn his eyes into fountains now finds them consumed. Wesley is blunt: he wept himself almost blind.

The poured-out liver divides the two who work on the words. Ellicott calls the phrase unparalleled but easily explained, the liver being thought of with the heart and bowels as a seat of intense feeling, whether joy or sorrow, and here giving way without restraint. Keil and Delitzsch report it variously explained and refuse the reading that makes the liver the fountain of blood and so the seat of animal life, denying the proverb usually cited will bear it — the same proverb Ellicott cites for his own account. Wesley solves it anatomically, putting the gall beneath the liver, and treats the verse as one long expression of affliction.

Gill and Calvin both stop to say who speaks in the cry for corn and wine. Not the sucklings, since infants cannot ask and are not given wine, but children somewhat grown, the two named together because one sort died in the streets and the other in the mother's bosom. Ellicott thinks the words paint what was passing before the writer's eye, though it may be the vivid present standing for the past: the children cried for food, their mothers had none, and they breathed out their lives clinging to the breast. Clarke draws it tighter, that in trying to draw nourishment from exhausted mothers they died in their bosoms.

The question about a witness is a question about comfort. Gill reads it as a demand for argument and evidence: what could be produced to show any nation was ever in such a case. Clarke prefers a rendering that makes it what shall I urge to thee, and gives the breach as a flood of afflictions, a sea of troubles, an ocean of miseries. Ellicott explains why the question has no answer: had there been a parallel, and had it been surmounted, it might have been cited in evidence and yielded some consolation; there being none, the ruin is illimitable as the ocean and past remedy. Calvin describes the convention refused. When we comfort a sick man we tell him he is neither the first nor the last, that many are like him, that the condition is common to mortals; the prophet asks what use such witnesses would be here. Wesley makes the breach one in a sea wall, where the water comes with a torrent no defence can be made against.

On the prophets the blame is placed differently. Keil and Delitzsch, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all charge the false prophets: they promised peace where there was none, did not expose the sin and guilt with a view to amendment, and so brought the calamity on instead of averting it; what they uttered as vision from God was itself a cause of banishment. Ellicott notes the ironic use of the word for burdens, the thing such men delighted in, and Gill supplies specimens: the vessels would come back within two years, and the city would not be given up. Calvin turns the charge round on the hearers. The Jews had been inebriated with flatteries and destroyed themselves as though wilfully drinking sweet poison; they sought to be deceived, cast themselves into the snare with avidity, and looked out flatterers for teachers.
15:
Gill separates the travellers who clap as they pass from the implacable enemies named next. Keil and Delitzsch make the gestures precise: clapping here is not the sign of anger it sometimes is but of delight at another's injury, hissing and head-shaking are scorn, and the question about the perfection of beauty is scornful astonishment. Ellicott says the enemies added bitterness by reminding her what she had been and setting it against what she was. Clarke doubts the title ever fitted the city, which was never fine or splendid, and gives it to the Temple, the most splendid building in the world. On the enemies' speech they note three verbs heaped without conjunctions, which suits an impassioned speaker, and that seeing here means living to see.

Clarke interrupts with an observation of a different kind: these two verses stand out of order, the earlier opening with the letter that should follow and the later with the letter that should come first, so the pair ought to be interchanged to keep the alphabet.

Against the boasting the writer names the real author. Gill says it was not so much the Chaldeans, whatever they ascribed to themselves. Keil and Delitzsch have God executing now what he threatened long ago and preparing the enemy's triumph himself, so he alone can bring help, and will, if entreated without ceasing. Ellicott finds an element of hope in what looks at first only terrible: it is better to fall into the hands of God than of men, and a suffering that comes as chastisement may be mitigated by repentance, the destroyer being also the healer. Calvin arrives by another road. When enemies insult us we feel it, but grief soon blunts the feeling; the remedy is to stop fixing our thoughts on the insolence of men and remember that the wicked are the scourges by which God chastises.

The address to the wall is the crux. Clarke says plainly that he does not know what it means, that it is harsh to tell a wall to let tears run down day and night, that there is no parallel for it, and that one of his most ancient manuscripts simply omits the three words, leaving a text that runs smoothly without them; he takes the exhortation for the words of passers-by urging the people to plead. Ellicott treats the boldness as deliberate, the wall being called on to take up its lamentation as though it were a human mourner, and still the one addressed in the next verse, watching the children die and lifting her hands in supplication for them. On whose heart cried, Gill reports a reading that makes it the enemies blaspheming, but prefers the Jews; Keil and Delitzsch rule the enemies out, since the suffix cannot point back to them.

Whether the cry was piety is Calvin's question, and his answer is no. There was no cry in their heart; the phrase only measures how much grief there was, since silence is the token of patience and a man overcome forgets himself and bursts out. He adds that this is a common cry which even the reprobate utter, nature teaching men to run to God under pressure, so that those with no fear of him will still ask for mercy in extremity. Gill leaves it open, that some no doubt cried sincerely and all wished to be preserved. On the night watches Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree the sense is at the head of each watch, so through the whole night rather than the first watch only, and Clarke pictures the watchmen sending up a prayer in place of calling the hour. Calvin explains why fugitives already driven off like sheep should be told to arise: they were lying torpid in their sins, and it is that sloth the summons is aimed at.
20:
The opening plea is read as an appeal to the covenant. Keil and Delitzsch take the question to mean not what innocent people are being sacrificed, a reading they name and reject, but to what nation: not a heathen one but the people of God's own choosing, to whom every promise had been given. Ellicott says the same briefly. Calvin also names an alternative and refuses it, that other interpreters make it a comparison, whether any people was ever so severely afflicted; he holds instead that the people set the covenant made with their fathers before God, as if to say that had he raged so against strangers there would be nothing to wonder at, but they are his heritage and peculiar people. Gill is careful that nothing is charged against God: the church neither accuses him of injustice nor complains of hard usage, but asks to be looked on with pity and leaves her case with him. Both he and Calvin note the words are supplied by the prophet as a prayer for others to use.

Clarke reads the question differently, as a father asked whether he will destroy his own offspring, and puts the horror in the clause that follows: was it ever heard that a mother devoured her own child, a helpless infant of a span long? He grants such distress in a siege had been foretold in the law, but thinks the fatherhood better supported by the context. Ellicott collects the parallels: it was predicted, it is the natural incident of a starving city, it had happened at another siege and would again under the Romans, and these words show it happened here.

The second horror is laid beside the first deliberately. Ellicott says the stress falls on it: the holiest place itself was profaned with the blood of God's own priests and prophets. Keil and Delitzsch make that murder the ground of the question, which is why it means what nation rather than what innocents.

From the sanctuary the lament moves outward. Ellicott has the mourner's thoughts turn from the massacre in the holy place to the slaughter done in every corner of the city. Gill has young and old lying promiscuously in the public streets, fainting for want of food or killed outright, the enemy sparing neither age nor sex. Calvin insists on the attribution: the text does not say they were slain by the enemy but by God, which was the hardest thing to get the Jews to accept, so filled were they with rage against the men who held the swords. Clarke supplies a parallel from a Roman poet on a civil war: nobility perishing with the common people, the sword ranging wide, blood standing in the temples and the stones slippery with slaughter, no man's age availing him; and remarks that the lines read as if translated from these very verses.

The last image is a summons. Gill has the terrors come at God's call as soldiers at their general's, in such numbers as men once came from all Judea to one of the three yearly feasts. Clarke and Wesley take it the same way, terrors called together to feast on the city as the people were once convoked to keep a festival; Calvin adds the trumpets sounded when a feast was at hand, and that the word for the assembly serves also for its place and time. Two of them stop over the tense. Keil and Delitzsch judge the imperfect was chosen only to satisfy the alphabet, the sense of custom or repetition not suiting here, and keep the description going. Calvin agrees the alphabet required it, notes that every version renders it as a past without saying why, and proposes reading it as a wish. Ellicott records a Greek rendering, followed by some, that turns the terrors round about into villages, and dismisses it.
